# How the early-warning model works: notes for staff who are not data specialists

Personal portfolio project on public UK distance-learning data; not affiliated with or endorsed by ITE or the Open
University. Written as knowledge-transfer material: what was done, why, and how to check it yourself.

<!-- Generated by scripts/build_docs.py from results/*.json. Edit docs/templates/model_explainer.md instead. -->

## The question

On a given day in term, which of the students still registered are most likely to end the module with a result of
Withdrawn or Fail? The answer is used only to order a contact list.

## The idea in one paragraph

Take last year's classes. For every student, write down what could be seen on day 28: how much they had clicked,
when they were last online, what they had handed in and how it was marked. We know how last year ended, so we can
let a statistical method find which of those early signs went with a bad ending. Then apply the same recipe to this
year's students on their day 28 and sort them by the result.

## What the model looks at

Twenty-four numbers per student, all known before the cut-off: totals and recent counts of clicks, days and weeks
active, days since last seen, clicks by kind of activity, clicks relative to the class median, assessments due,
submitted, missed and late, average score, results carried over from an earlier attempt, earlier attempts at the
module, credits being studied, how early the student registered, and prior education level.

What it is deliberately not given: gender, age band, disability, region and deprivation band; the date a student
unregistered; and the final result.

## Two ways of cheating by accident, and how they are ruled out

**Using the future.** If the "clicks so far" on day 28 quietly included day 40, the model would look brilliant and be
useless. Two checks:

1. The data is replayed week by week. The day-28 features were saved in the week they would have been produced,
   before later weeks had been loaded, and they equal the features rebuilt afterwards on all
   {{pipeline.json:asof_equivalence.rows_compared|int}} rows.
2. A detector rewrites everything after the cut-off (later clicks, later marks, later withdrawals, all results) and
   rebuilds the features. Nothing may change. When a future-looking feature is planted on purpose, the detector
   names it.

**Using the answer.** The unregistration date is the withdrawal outcome under another name. It is used only to decide
who is still registered on the cut-off day, never as an input.

A third, subtler one: the same person can take a module twice. If they were in both the practice data and the test
data the model could recognise them. {{model.json:cutoffs.28.split.train_rows_dropped_for_overlap|int}} such rows
were removed from the 2013 side at day 28.

## How it is judged

Not by accuracy. Accuracy rewards saying "nobody is at risk" when few are. Three questions instead:

| Question | Measure | Day 28, gradient boosting | Day 28, logistic regression |
|---|---|---|---|
| Does it put at-risk students near the top of the list? | PR-AUC (1 is perfect; {{model.json:cutoffs.28.models.gradient_boosting.prevalence|.2f}} is what random ordering scores here) | {{model.json:cutoffs.28.models.gradient_boosting.pr_auc|.3f}} | {{model.json:cutoffs.28.models.logistic_regression.pr_auc|.3f}} |
| If we contact the top 20%, how many are truly at risk? | Precision at 20% | {{model.json:cutoffs.28.models.gradient_boosting.top20.precision|pct0}} | {{model.json:cutoffs.28.models.logistic_regression.top20.precision|pct0}} |
| And what share of all at-risk students did we reach? | Recall at 20% | {{model.json:cutoffs.28.models.gradient_boosting.top20.recall|pct0}} | {{model.json:cutoffs.28.models.logistic_regression.top20.recall|pct0}} |
| When it says 0.7, does about 70% turn out at risk? | Brier score (lower is better; always guessing the average scores {{model.json:cutoffs.28.models.gradient_boosting.brier_of_constant_prevalence|.3f}}) | {{model.json:cutoffs.28.models.gradient_boosting.brier|.3f}} | {{model.json:cutoffs.28.models.logistic_regression.brier|.3f}} |

Every figure comes with an interval from resampling the students, because a different class would give a slightly
different number.

## Is a complicated model worth it?

Compared with two rules anyone could apply by hand and with a simple model:

{{table:model}}

Early in term the more flexible model (gradient boosting) orders students better. By day 56 the simple one (logistic
regression) is as good for the purpose of picking the top 20%. The dashboard uses the simple one, because each
student's score can be broken into named parts: that is where the "reasons" come from.

## Does it treat groups differently?

The model does not see protected attributes, but it can still flag one group more readily than another. The share
of truly at-risk students who get flagged is compared between groups in the README. At day 28 the largest gap is
{{model.json:cutoffs.28.fairness_gradient_boosting.age_band.recall_gap|pct1}} between age bands (the 55-and-over
group is small) and {{model.json:cutoffs.28.fairness_gradient_boosting.gender.recall_gap|pct1}} between men and
women. These gaps are reported, not corrected. Whether a gap is acceptable is a decision for the institution, not
for the model.

## How to check a claim yourself

- `python -m pytest tests/test_features.py -q` runs the leakage checks and the hand-worked examples.
- `tests/helpers.py` holds a seven-student class small enough to work out every feature on paper.
- `results/model.json` holds every number on this page.

## What this model cannot tell you

- Why a student is struggling.
- Whether contacting them helps. That needs a record of who was contacted and what happened next.
- Anything about students at another institution, in another mode of study, or in another decade.
